active_paradigms.idea: Replace width-8 beam truncation with best-first branch-and-bound over transaction prefixes using heapq
active_paradigms.description: The current program evaluates true simulator cost for every beam extension, which is valuable, but it irrevocably discards all but eight prefixes based only on their current partial cost. Use a priority queue of prefix states instead: each state contains an ordered prefix, remaining transactions, and `workload.get_opt_seq_cost(prefix)`. This partial cost is a valid lower bound if adding transactions cannot reduce already induced precedence delays, so prune a state whenever its bound is at least the best complete schedule found. Obtain a strong incumbent early from the existing greedy/beam construction, then expand the lowest-bound live state first. Branch transaction choices in an informed order, such as trying extensions with the lowest immediate simulator cost first, so high-quality complete schedules are found early and make pruning effective. For small transaction counts this becomes exact rather than heuristic; for larger instances, impose a node budget and return the best incumbent, which still avoids the arbitrary width-8 failure mode. This directly addresses the main weakness of the current algorithm: two prefixes with similar current cost can have radically different achievable final makespans, yet one is currently discarded permanently.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The returned makespan from `workload.get_opt_seq_cost`; prioritize finding a globally optimal permutation whenever the search tree can be exhausted, while retaining an anytime best schedule under a search budget.
active_paradigms.cautions: Validate monotonicity of partial-prefix cost before relying on it as a pruning bound; if the simulator's partial cost can decrease after an extension, use it only as a queue priority and do not prune from it. Store immutable tuple prefixes in queue states and use a deterministic tie-break counter because Python cannot compare arbitrary equal-priority state payloads. Set a practical expansion cap for large workloads, since worst-case permutation search remains exponential.

active_paradigms.idea: Use disconnected conflict-component decomposition with NetworkX before searching orderings
active_paradigms.description: Build the transaction conflict graph directly from the workload: connect two transactions if they access a common key and at least one access is a write. The present beam search treats every transaction as globally coupled, even though transactions in distinct graph components have no read-write or write-write dependency and therefore their relative order cannot create a conflict edge. Call `networkx.connected_components` on this graph and solve the ordering inside each nontrivial component independently, using an exact search or a substantially wider beam because each subproblem is much smaller. Transactions with no conflict edges may be placed anywhere and should not consume search effort. Concatenate the component schedules in a deterministic order, then evaluate the resulting full schedule once with the real simulator; optionally test the small number of component-order permutations when there are few components, because this is cheap and protects against undocumented simulator behavior. This is fundamentally different from tuning the beam: it reduces the dimension of the actual combinatorial problem by exploiting exact independence. It is especially valuable when workloads are formed from several key clusters, where global factorial search is unnecessary.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Makespan indirectly through exact removal of irrelevant cross-component ordering decisions, allowing much stronger optimization of conflict-dense components within the same evaluation-time budget.
active_paradigms.cautions: A graph edge must be added only for pairs sharing a key for which at least one transaction writes; read-read sharing is not a conflict. Inspect the available Workload transaction representation carefully and parse operation strings only if no structured operation list is exposed. Do not assume component concatenation is safe without one full-cost check; if simulator semantics include a global resource beyond data conflicts, retain a final cross-component ordering check.

active_paradigms.idea: Use randomized iterated local search with shuffle-based diverse restarts and full swap/block neighborhoods
active_paradigms.description: The current code starts from a single narrow-beam solution and accepts only strictly improving one-transaction relocations, so it stops at the first insertion-local optimum. Use `random.shuffle` to generate diverse transaction permutations or diverse tie orders, refine each with simulator-evaluated local search, and retain the best complete schedule across `num_seqs` restarts. Within a restart, evaluate both pairwise swaps and remove-and-reinsert moves; swaps are important because a beneficial exchange can require moving both transactions, while the current first-improvement relocation may require a temporary worsening move and cannot cross that barrier. Use best-improvement selection per local-search pass rather than committing to the first detected improvement, then repeat until neither neighborhood improves. Seed some restarts from the beam solution after a substantial random perturbation, and seed others from completely shuffled schedules, so the search explores both nearby and distant basins. Every acceptance decision must use `workload.get_opt_seq_cost` on the complete candidate, not proxy statistics such as transaction length or write count. This turns `num_seqs` into actual diversification budget and is robust when a full branch-and-bound search is too expensive.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Best complete-schedule makespan over multiple independent local-optimum basins; this specifically targets improvements unavailable to strict single-start insertion descent.
active_paradigms.cautions: Cache evaluated complete permutation tuples during a restart or globally to avoid repeatedly invoking the simulator for the same swap/insertion result. Keep randomization reproducible with a fixed seed unless the benchmark intentionally rewards stochastic variation. Full swap plus all insertion evaluations cost O(n^3) simulator calls per pass, so cap passes or use candidate lists for very large n; never replace final candidate evaluation with a heuristic estimate.
